06.01.title: Stress
06.01.html:
Statics told you the forces in a bike frame tube or a rail. It didn’t tell you whether the tube survives. A 2 kN force is nothing for a thick steel bar and fatal for a thin wire. What matters is how the force is spread over the material, and that is stress. This lesson defines it properly, as the thing that gives the force per area on any cut through a body.

Force per area on a cut

Cut a loaded body with a plane through a point, with unit normal n. The material on one side pushes and pulls on the other. Over a tiny area ΔA it exerts a force ΔF. The traction vector is

t(n)=ΔA→0lim​ΔAΔF​[N/m2=Pa; engineers use MPa=N/mm2].

Its component along n is the normal stress σn​=t⋅n (tension positive). The part in the plane is the shear stress τ. The traction depends on the plane you choose: the same point can carry pure tension on one plane and mostly shear on another.

The stress tensor

Cauchy’s result: you don’t need to know t on every plane. Nine numbers, the tractions on the three coordinate planes, give all the others:

t=σn,σ=​σxx​τxy​τxz​​τxy​σyy​τyz​​τxz​τyz​σzz​​​.

The proof is equilibrium of a tiny tetrahedron with three faces on the coordinate planes and one with normal n. Moment equilibrium of a tiny cube makes σ symmetric, so only six numbers are independent. Column j of σ is the traction on the plane with normal ej​.

Worked exampleA 3D stress state in a frame lug

σ=​80300​30−200​0010​​ MPa, plane normal n=(1,1,1)/3​.

  1. t=σn=(110,10,10)/3​=(63.51,5.77,5.77) MPa.
  2. Normal stress σn​=t⋅n=130/3=43.33 MPa.
  3. Shear τ=∣t∣2−σn2​​=47.14 MPa. On this plane the shear is larger than the tension.
  4. In 2D, a tube with 60 MPa axial and 25 MPa shear: the plane at 30° carries 66.65 MPa normal stress. Scanning every angle, the largest normal stress is 69.05 MPa, exactly the largest eigenvalue of σ (more in 06.07).

Exercise 1A tie rod

A steel tie rod of 16 mm diameter carries 30 kN. Find the axial stress, then the normal and shear stress on a plane cut at 45° to the axis.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A=π⋅82=201.1 mm², so σ=30000/201.1=149.2 MPa.
  2. In the rod, σ=diag(149.2,0). With n=(cos45°,sin45°): t=(105.5,0) MPa.
  3. σn​=105.5⋅0.7071=74.6 MPa and τ=74.6 MPa: half the axial stress each. Ductile metals in tension fail by slip on such planes, which is why their fractures show 45° shear lips.

06.02.title: Strain
06.02.html:
Stress is what the material feels; strain is what you can measure. A strain gauge glued to a bridge girder or a bike crank reads how much the material stretches and distorts, and from that, via Hooke’s law, engineers infer the stress. This lesson defines strain from the displacement field and shows its one subtle point: rotations must not count as strain.

Displacement and its gradient

Every material point moves by a displacement u(x). A uniform u is a rigid translation: no deformation. What matters is how u changes from point to point, the displacement gradient ∇u with entries ∂ui​/∂xj​. Split it into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part:

∇u=ε (strain)21​(∇u+∇uT)​​+ω (rotation)21​(∇u−∇uT)​​.
  • εxx​=∂ux​/∂x is the stretch of a fibre along x (0.001 = 0.1 % = 1000 microstrain).
  • εxy​=21​(∂ux​/∂y+∂uy​/∂x) is half the change of a right angle. Engineers often use γxy​=2εxy​.
  • ω is a small rigid rotation and causes no stress.

Small strain and its limit

This small-strain tensor is linear in u, which makes everything downstream (beams, finite elements) linear. The price: a rigid rotation by θ shows up as a false strain of about −θ2/2. For rotations of a degree or less, that’s negligible. For a fishing rod or a rubber seal, you need large-deformation measures (such as the Green–Lagrange strain, which is exactly zero for any rigid rotation).

Worked exampleStrains from a displacement field

The code samples displacement fields on a 101 × 101 grid and differentiates them numerically.

  1. ux​=0.002x+0.0005y, uy​=0.0005x−0.0006y: εxx​=0.002, εyy​=−0.0006, εxy​=21​(0.0005+0.0005)=0.0005, rotation zero.
  2. A rigid rotation by 0.01 rad gives ∣εxx​∣=1−cos0.01=5.0×10−5, matching θ2/2. At 0.001 rad it falls 100 times, to 5×10−7: second order.
  3. A bending-like field ux​=−kxy, uy​=kx2/2 gives εxx​=−ky, varying linearly through the depth, with zero shear strain. That’s the beam theory of 06.09 in miniature.

Exercise 1A strain gauge rosette

Three gauges on a bike crank read ε0​=600×10−6 along x, ε90​=−180×10−6 along y, and ε45​=410×10−6 at 45°. Find γxy​. (The strain along a direction at angle φ is εxx​cos2φ+εyy​sin2φ+γxy​sinφcosφ.)

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At 45°: ε45​=21​(εxx​+εyy​)+21​γxy​.
  2. 410=21​(600−180)+21​γxy​=210+21​γxy​, so γxy​=400×10−6.
  3. That’s how every 45° rosette on a test rig works: three readings give the full 2D strain state.

quiz.explain: Half the sum of the cross derivatives.

06.03.title: Hooke's law
06.03.html:
Stress and strain are linked by the material. For most engineering metals at working loads, and for bamboo along its fibres, the link is linear and reversible: double the load, double the stretch, unload and it springs back. That is Hooke’s law, and two numbers capture it for an isotropic material. This lesson builds the full 3D version as a 6 × 6 matrix and runs a virtual tensile test on it.

One dimension

Pull a bar: the axial strain is proportional to the stress, σ=Eε, with Young’s modulus E. The bar also gets thinner. The ratio of lateral contraction to axial stretch is Poisson’s ratio ν:

εlat​=−νεax​.

Typical values: steel E=210 GPa, ν=0.30; aluminium 70 GPa, 0.33; bamboo along the culm around 18 GPa (but far softer across it). For isotropic materials, ν lies between −1 and 0.5; rubber is close to 0.5 (nearly incompressible).

Three dimensions

Superpose the three directions and add shear, τ=Gγ:

εxx​=E1​[σxx​−ν(σyy​+σzz​)],γxy​=Gτxy​​,G=2(1+ν)E​.

Inverted, with the Lamé constants λ=(1+ν)(1−2ν)Eν​ and μ=G:

σ=λtr(ε)I+2με.

In Voigt notation the six stresses and six strains (with engineering shear strains) become vectors and the law becomes σ=Cε with a 6 × 6 matrix. Finite element programs store exactly that. The bulk modulus K=E/(3(1−2ν)) links pressure to volume change: ΔV/V=−p/K.

Worked exampleA virtual tensile test

The code builds C from E and ν, applies σxx​=100 MPa alone, and solves for the strains.

  1. Steel: λ=121.15 GPa, G=80.77 GPa, K=175 GPa. The test returns E=210 GPa and ν=0.3 exactly, with εyy​=εzz​ and no shear strain.
  2. Aluminium: G=26.32 GPa, K=68.63 GPa.
  3. 100 MPa hydrostatic pressure on steel: volume strain −100/175000=−5.71×10−4.
  4. A 300 mm steel bar of 20 mm diameter at 100 MPa gets 0.143 mm longer and 2.86 µm thinner.

Exercise 1A rubber pad and a steel block

A cube is squeezed with 10 MPa on the top face while its sides are free. Compare the lateral expansion of steel (E=210 GPa, ν=0.3) and of rubber (E=5 MPa, ν=0.49), as strains.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Steel: εax​=−10/210000=−4.76×10−5, lateral +0.3⋅4.76×10−5=1.43×10−5.
  2. Rubber: εax​=−10/5=−2. That’s far beyond small strain, so the linear law no longer applies, which is the real lesson. At 0.1 MPa instead, εax​=−0.02 and lateral +0.0098: the rubber bulges almost as much as it shortens, keeping its volume.

quiz.q: Shear modulus G (GPa) of steel, E=210 GPa, ν=0.3. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: E/(2(1+ν)).

quiz.q: Bulk modulus K (GPa) of steel.
quiz.explain: E/(3(1−2ν)).

quiz.q: Strain (microstrain) of aluminium at 140 MPa, E=70 GPa.
quiz.explain: σ/E.

quiz.q: Lamé constant λ (GPa) for steel. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: Eν/((1+ν)(1−2ν)).

quiz.q: A material with ν close to 0.5 is…
quiz.explain: K→∞ as ν→0.5.

06.04.title: Axial bars
06.04.html:
Rods, cables, bolts, truss members and brake cables mostly carry axial force. How much they stretch matters: a brake lever that travels too far feels spongy, a bolt that stretches loses clamping force, and a lift cable that stretches lets the cabin bounce. For a bar the answer is one formula, and this lesson extends it to stepped and tapered bars and to self-weight.

The bar formula

A bar of length L, area A and modulus E carrying an axial force N has stress σ=N/A and strain ε=σ/E. Uniform strain means the elongation is

δ=εL=EANL​.

EA is the axial stiffness of the section and EA/L the spring stiffness of the bar. When N, A or E change along the bar, add up the pieces, or integrate:

δ=i∑​Ei​Ai​Ni​Li​​,δ=∫0L​EA(x)N(x)​dx.

Find each segment’s internal force Ni​ by a cut and an FBD (lesson 05.06), then add the stretches.

Self-weight and tapers

A cable of density ρ hanging under its own weight carries N(x)=ρgA(L−x), so δ=ρgL2/(2E), independent of the area. A round bar tapering linearly from radius r1​ to r2​ gives δ=PL/(Eπr1​r2​).

Worked exampleA brake cable and a stepped bar

  1. The brake cable from lesson 05.12: steel, 1.5 mm diameter, 1.8 m, 168 N. A=1.767 mm², σ=95.1 MPa, δ=168⋅1800/(200000⋅1.767)=0.856 mm. (Stranded cable is softer than solid wire, so the real figure is larger.)
  2. Stepped bar fixed at a wall: steel 400 mm × Ø20 next to the wall, aluminium 300 mm × Ø30 beyond it. 30 kN pulls at the free end, 10 kN pushes back at the joint. Cuts give N=20 kN in the steel and 30 kN in the aluminium.
  3. δ=20000⋅400/(210000⋅314.2)+30000⋅300/(70000⋅706.9)=0.1213+0.1819=0.3032 mm.
  4. A 1 km steel cable hanging free stretches 7850⋅9.81⋅10002/(2⋅210×109)=0.183 m under its own weight.

Exercise 1A lift rod

A 6 m steel hanger rod of 24 mm diameter carries a 45 kN floor load at its lower end. Find the stress and the stretch. What diameter keeps the stretch under 2 mm?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A=π⋅122=452.4 mm², σ=45000/452.4=99.5 MPa.
  2. δ=45000⋅6000/(210000⋅452.4)=2.84 mm.
  3. For δ≤2 mm: A≥45000⋅6000/(210000⋅2)=642.9 mm², so d≥28.6 mm. Use 30 mm.

quiz.explain: NL/(EA).

06.05.title: Statically indeterminate bars
06.05.html:
Lesson 05.08 flagged structures where statics alone can’t find the forces. Now you have the missing ingredient: deformation. A bar clamped between two walls, a steel bolt inside an aluminium sleeve, a concrete column with steel bars inside it. All are solved with the same three-step recipe, and the answers say something important: stiffness attracts load.

The three ingredients

  1. Equilibrium: the force equations you’d write anyway. They have more unknowns than equations.
  2. Compatibility: a geometric condition on the deformations. For a bar between rigid walls, the total stretch must be zero. For parts bolted together, they must stretch by the same amount.
  3. Constitutive law: Hooke’s law, δ=NL/(EA), links forces to deformations.

Put the force–deformation law into the compatibility condition and you get the extra equations you need.

A bar between two walls

A bar between rigid walls carries a load P at the point where part 1 (length a, stiffness E1​A1​, at wall A) meets part 2 (length b, stiffness E2​A2​, at wall B). Part 1 is in tension RA​ and part 2 in compression RB​.

RA​+RB​=P,E1​A1​RA​a​=E2​A2​RB​b​.

For a uniform bar, RA​=Pb/L and RB​=Pa/L: the wall closer to the load takes more. In general each part takes load in proportion to its spring stiffness EA/L. That is the principle behind every indeterminate structure: load goes where the stiffness is.

Stiffness matrices

The same answer comes from treating each part as a spring with stiffness k=EA/L, assembling a stiffness matrix and solving Ku=f for the free nodal displacements. That is the 1D finite element method, which the code uses as a cross-check, and it scales to any number of parts and loads.

Worked exampleTwo walls, two materials

  1. Uniform steel bar, L=1000 mm, 60 kN at a=300 mm: RA​=60⋅700/1000=42 kN, RB​=18 kN. The load point moves 42000⋅300/(210000⋅400)=0.15 mm.
  2. Steel 300 mm (A=400 mm²) next to wall A and aluminium 700 mm (A=600 mm²) next to wall B. Flexibilities a/(E1​A1​)=3.571×10−6 and b/(E2​A2​)=1.667×10−5 mm/N.
  3. RA​=60⋅16.667/(3.571+16.667)=49.41 kN and RB​=10.59 kN. The short steel part carries 123.5 MPa, the long aluminium part only 17.6 MPa.
  4. With 25 kN and 8 kN at two points on a three-part bar, the stiffness model gives reactions 24.23 and 8.77 kN, summing to the 33 kN applied.

Exercise 1A bolt and a sleeve

A steel bolt (A=80 mm²) passes through an aluminium sleeve (A=240 mm²) of the same length. A 30 kN compressive load is applied to both through rigid end plates. How is the load shared?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Equilibrium: Ns​+Na​=30 kN.
  2. Compatibility: same length, same shortening, so Ns​/(Es​As​)=Na​/(Ea​Aa​).
  3. Stiffnesses: Es​As​=210000⋅80=16.8 MN and Ea​Aa​=70000⋅240=16.8 MN. Equal, so each carries 15 kN. Stresses: 187.5 MPa in the bolt and 62.5 MPa in the sleeve. Equal force, very different stress.

quiz.explain: Pb/L.

quiz.explain: Load in proportion to stiffness.

quiz.explain: Half the load on 80 mm².

06.06.title: Thermal stress
06.06.html:
Swiss railway tracks are welded into continuous rails hundreds of metres long. On a hot summer afternoon the steel wants to grow by several centimetres, and it can’t. The result is a large compressive force in the rail, with no load on the track at all. Thermal stress like this cracks engine blocks, buckles rails and breaks glass, and it follows from one extra term in Hooke’s law.

Thermal strain

A free bar heated by ΔT expands by a strain εth​=αΔT, without any stress. α is the coefficient of thermal expansion: about 12×10−6/K for steel, 23×10−6/K for aluminium, 9×10−6/K for glass. The total strain is the sum of a mechanical and a thermal part:

ε=Eσ​+αΔT.

Constrained expansion

If the bar can’t change length at all, ε=0 and

σ=−EαΔT.

That doesn’t depend on the bar’s length or area. For steel, Eα≈2.4 MPa per kelvin: 30 K of heating gives about 72 MPa of compression. A strain gauge on that rail reads zero, since the total strain is zero. The stress is real but the strain is invisible.

If the bar can move a little first (an expansion gap g in a bar of length L), it expands freely until the gap closes, at ΔT=g/(αL). Beyond that, only the extra expansion is resisted: σ=−E(αΔTL−g)/L.

Rails and buckling

Continuous welded rail is laid and clamped at a neutral temperature well above the yearly average, often around 25 °C in central Europe. Cold days then put the rail in tension, which steel handles well. Very hot days put it in compression, and the track can buckle sideways (“sun kink”) if the sleepers and ballast don’t hold it. That’s why track crews check ballast shoulders before summer.

Worked exampleA welded rail through the seasons

UIC 60 rail, A=7686 mm², E=210 GPa, α=11.5×10−6/K, neutral temperature 25 °C.

  1. Rail at 55 °C in the sun: σ=−210000⋅11.5×10−6⋅30=−72.45 MPa. Force 72.45⋅7686=557 kN of compression.
  2. Rail at −20 °C: ΔT=−45 K, σ=+108.7 MPa, 835 kN of tension.
  3. Old jointed track: 25 m rails with 5 mm gaps laid at 10 °C. The gaps close at 5/(11.5×10−6⋅25000)=17.4 K above laying temperature. At 30 °C the rail is under only 6.3 MPa; at 45 °C, 42.5 MPa.

Exercise 1A brass bushing

A brass bushing (E=100 GPa, α=19×10−6/K) is pressed between two rigid steel plates at 20 °C with no initial stress. The machine runs at 80 °C. Ignoring the plates' own expansion, what stress develops in the bushing? Brass yields at about 200 MPa; is it safe?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. σ=−EαΔT=−100000⋅19×10−6⋅60=−114 MPa.
  2. Below 200 MPa, so it doesn’t yield, but with a safety factor of only 1.75. Steel plates would expand too (α≈12×10−6/K), so the real stress is set by the difference in α: about 100000⋅7×10−6⋅60=42 MPa.

06.07.title: Stress transformation and Mohr's circle
06.07.html:
Lesson 06.01 showed that the normal and shear stress depend on which plane you look at. A designer wants to know the worst plane: the largest tension (where a brittle part cracks) and the largest shear (where a ductile part yields). For plane stress, a 19th-century graphical trick by Otto Mohr shows all planes at once as points on a circle, and it’s still the clearest way to think about it.

Rotating the element

For plane stress (σx​,σy​,τxy​), the stresses on a face whose normal is rotated by θ are

σx′​=2σx​+σy​​+2σx​−σy​​cos2θ+τxy​sin2θ,τx′y′​=−2σx​−σy​​sin2θ+τxy​cos2θ.

The double angle is the key. Square and add the two equations and θ disappears:

(σx′​−C)2+τx′y′2​=R2,C=2σx​+σy​​,R=(2σx​−σy​​)2+τxy2​​.

Every orientation lies on one circle in the (σ,τ) plane: Mohr’s circle.

Reading the circle

  • Principal stresses: σ1,2​=C±R, where the circle crosses the σ axis. On those planes the shear is zero.
  • Principal angle: tan2θp​=2τxy​/(σx​−σy​).
  • Maximum in-plane shear: τmax​=R, on planes at 45° to the principal ones.
  • Rotating the element by θ moves its point by 2θ round the circle.
  • σx​+σy​=σ1​+σ2​ doesn’t change with orientation (an invariant).

Mathematically the principal stresses are the eigenvalues of σ and the principal directions its eigenvectors. In 3D there are three, and three circles.

Worked exampleA frame lug in plane stress

σx​=80, σy​=−20, τxy​=30 MPa.

  1. C=30 MPa, R=502+302​=58.31 MPa.
  2. σ1​=88.31 MPa, σ2​=−28.31 MPa, matching the eigenvalues of σ.
  3. θp​=21​arctan(60/100)=15.48°. Rotating the element by that angle makes the shear vanish.
  4. τmax​=58.31 MPa. The code also checks that 12 rotated states all lie on the circle and keep σx​+σy​=60 MPa.
  5. The bike tube (60 MPa axial, 25 MPa shear) has σ1​=69.05 MPa at 19.90°.

Exercise 1A twisted shaft

A shaft in pure torsion has τxy​=50 MPa and no normal stress. Find the principal stresses and their directions. Why do chalk sticks twisted to failure break along a helix?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. C=0, R=50 MPa, so σ1​=50 MPa and σ2​=−50 MPa.
  2. tan2θp​=100/0→∞, so θp​=45°.
  3. Chalk is brittle and fails in tension, across the direction of σ1​. That direction runs at 45° round the stick, so the crack follows a 45° helix. A ductile steel shaft fails instead on the plane of maximum shear, straight across.

06.08.title: Failure criteria
06.08.html:
A tensile test gives one number: the yield stress fy​, where a bar under pure tension starts to deform permanently. A real part, like a shaft under bending and torsion, has a combination of stresses. Is 120 MPa of tension plus 70 MPa of shear safe for a steel with fy​=355 MPa? A failure criterion turns any stress state into one equivalent stress you can compare with fy​.

Why shear matters for metals

Metals yield by crystal planes slipping over each other, which is driven by shear. Pure hydrostatic pressure, however large, causes no slip and no yield. So a good criterion for ductile metals must ignore the hydrostatic part of the stress and depend only on the deviatoric part, s=σ−31​tr(σ)I.

Tresca: maximum shear

Yield starts when the largest shear stress reaches its value in the tensile test, fy​/2:

σTresca​=σ1​−σ3​≤fy​.

von Mises: distortion energy

Split the strain energy into a volume-change part and a shape-change (distortion) part. Yield starts when the distortion energy reaches its value in the tensile test:

σvM​=21​[(σ1​−σ2​)2+(σ2​−σ3​)2+(σ3​−σ1​)2]​≤fy​.

For a shaft surface with normal stress σ and shear τ, these become σ2+3τ2​ (von Mises) and σ2+4τ2​ (Tresca). In pure shear, von Mises predicts yield at τ=fy​/3​=0.577fy​ and Tresca at 0.5fy​. Experiments on steel usually land closer to von Mises, which is why most design codes use it. Tresca is a little conservative and easier by hand.

In the σ1​–σ2​ plane (with σ3​=0), von Mises is an ellipse and Tresca a hexagon inscribed in it. Brittle materials like cast iron or glass need different criteria based on the largest tensile stress.

Worked exampleA drive shaft surface in S355

σ=120 MPa from bending, τ=70 MPa from torsion, fy​=355 MPa.

  1. von Mises: 1202+3⋅702​=170.59 MPa. Safety factor 355/170.59=2.08.
  2. Tresca: 1202+4⋅702​=184.39 MPa. Safety factor 1.93.
  3. Pure shear in S355: yield at τ=204.96 MPa (von Mises) or 177.5 MPa (Tresca).
  4. The code checks that the stress state and a tensile bar at 170.59 MPa store exactly the same distortion energy, and that 500 MPa of hydrostatic pressure gives an equivalent stress of zero.

Exercise 1A pressurised tube

A thin steel tube has hoop stress 180 MPa, axial stress 90 MPa and negligible radial stress. It’s made of S355. Find both equivalent stresses and the safety factors.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Principal stresses: σ1​=180, σ2​=90, σ3​=0 MPa.
  2. Tresca: 180−0=180 MPa, factor 1.97.
  3. von Mises: 21​[902+902+1802]​=24300​=155.9 MPa, factor 2.28.
  4. Note the third principal stress (zero, radial) matters for Tresca: the largest shear here is out of the plane.

06.09.title: Beam bending
06.09.html:
Lesson 05.13 gave the bending moment along a beam. This lesson turns a moment into stress, the step that decides whether a bamboo beam in a Bali pavilion, a floor joist or a bike handlebar holds. It’s the most used formula in structural and mechanical design, and it rests on one geometric assumption.

Plane sections remain plane

Euler–Bernoulli beam theory assumes that cross-sections stay flat and perpendicular to the bent axis. A bent beam then curves with radius ρ, and a fibre at distance y above the neutral axis shortens in proportion to y:

εx​=−ρy​=−κy.

That’s the bending field you saw in 06.02. With Hooke’s law, σx​=−Eκy: stress varies linearly across the depth, zero on the neutral axis.

Equilibrium of the section

Two conditions fix everything:

  • No axial force: ∫σdA=0, so the neutral axis passes through the centroid (05.17).
  • The stresses add up to the moment: M=−∫σydA=Eκ∫y2dA=EκI.

With I=∫y2dA, the second moment of area:

κ=EIM​,σ=−IMy​,σmax​=IMc​=WM​,

where c is the distance to the outermost fibre and W=I/c is the section modulus. For a rectangle b×h: I=bh3/12, W=bh2/6. Depth counts with its square, so a plank is far stronger on edge than flat.

Worked exampleA joist and a bamboo culm

  1. Timber joist 50 × 200 mm with M=6 kN m: I=50⋅2003/12=3.333×107 mm⁴, σmax​=6×106⋅100/3.333×107=18 MPa. The code integrates the stress field and gets zero axial force and exactly 6 kN m back.
  2. Bamboo culm, outer diameter 100 mm, wall 8 mm, 3 m span, 2 kN at mid-span: M=PL/4=1.5 kN m.
  3. I=π(1004−844)/64=2.465×106 mm⁴, so σmax​=1.5×106⋅50/2.465×106=30.4 MPa, comfortably below bamboo’s bending strength (typically above 100 MPa).
  4. The same amount of bamboo as a solid rod (54.3 mm diameter) would reach 95.7 MPa: 3.1 times higher. Nature’s hollow tube is no accident.

Exercise 1A handlebar

An aluminium handlebar is a tube, 22.2 mm outside diameter, 2 mm wall. A rider pulls up with 400 N at 0.25 m from the stem clamp (a cantilever). Find the bending stress at the clamp.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. M=400⋅250=1×105 N mm.
  2. d=18.2 mm, I=π(22.24−18.24)/64=6.54×103 mm⁴.
  3. σ=1×105⋅11.1/6537=170 MPa. That’s a large fraction of a typical 6061-T6 yield stress (about 275 MPa), and under repeated loading fatigue governs, which is why real bars are thicker or bulged at the clamp.

quiz.explain: bh2/6.

06.10.title: Second moment of area
06.10.html:
Steel beams are I-shaped, bike frames are tubes and bamboo grows hollow, all for the same reason. Bending stiffness and strength depend on the second moment of area I, which weights each bit of material by the square of its distance from the neutral axis. Put material far from the axis and you get much more stiffness for the same weight. This lesson builds a section calculator and compares shapes at equal area.

Definition and basic shapes

I=∫A​y2dA[mm4].
  • Rectangle b×h about its centroid: bh3/12.
  • Solid circle of diameter D: πD4/64.
  • Tube: π(D4−d4)/64.

The parallel-axis theorem

A part with area Ai​ and its own centroidal Ii​, whose centroid sits a distance di​ from the section’s neutral axis, contributes

I=i∑​(Ii​+Ai​di2​).

The Ad2 term is why flanges are so effective: for an I-beam almost all of I comes from the flanges' distance from the axis, while the thin web mainly carries shear and holds the flanges apart.

For any polygon, Green’s theorem gives the second moment directly from the vertices, Ix0​=121​∑(yi2​+yi​yi+1​+yi+12​)(xi​yi+1​−xi+1​yi​), which makes a good independent check.

Efficiency

Stiffness is EI and strength is W=I/c. At equal area (equal mass per metre), an I-section or a thin tube beats a solid square or round bar many times over. The limit is local buckling: a too-thin flange or tube wall crumples (lessons 06.19 and 06.20).

Worked exampleAn I-beam and friends

  1. I-section like an IPE 200 (without root fillets): h=200, b=100, tf​=8.5, tw​=5.6 mm. A=2724.8 mm².
  2. Flanges: 2[100⋅8.53/12+850⋅95.752]=1.5596×107 mm⁴. Web: 5.6⋅1833/12=2.860×106 mm⁴. Total I=1.8456×107 mm⁴. The polygon formula agrees.
  3. At the same area: square 6.19×105, round bar 5.91×105, tube 100 mm × 9.59 mm 2.82×106 mm⁴. The I-section is 29.8 times the square.
  4. The T-section from 05.17 (centroid 139.05 mm up) has I=4.03×107 mm⁴.

Exercise 1A box section

A steel box section is 150 mm wide, 200 mm deep, with 10 mm walls all round. Find I about the horizontal axis.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Outer rectangle minus inner: I=(150⋅2003−130⋅1803)/12.
  2. =(1.2×109−7.582×108)/12=3.682×107 mm⁴.
  3. Its area is 150⋅200−130⋅180=6600 mm². A solid square of that area would have I=66002/12=3.63×106 mm⁴, about ten times less.

06.11.title: Beam deflection
06.11.html:
A floor that is strong enough can still feel bouncy, a machine bed that bends ruins accuracy, and a footbridge that sags looks unsafe even when it isn’t. Stiffness is often the real design limit, not strength. This lesson computes how far a beam bends, by integrating the curvature from 06.09 and by solving the fourth-order beam equation directly.

The beam equation

With w(x) the deflection (upward positive) and small slopes, curvature is w′′, and 06.09 gave κ=M/EI:

EIw′′=M(x).

Combine with dM/dx=V and dV/dx=−q from 05.13, and for constant EI:

EIw′′′′=−q(x)(q downward positive).

Four integrations need four boundary conditions, two at each end:

End Conditions
Clamped w=0, w′=0
Pinned or roller w=0, M=0 (so w′′=0)
Free M=0, V=0 (w′′=0, w′′′=0)

Standard results

Integrating by hand (or in code) gives the cases every engineer knows:

  • Cantilever, tip load: δ=3EIPL3​.
  • Simply supported, central load: δ=48EIPL3​.
  • Simply supported, uniform load: δ=384EI5qL4​.

Note the powers: doubling the span multiplies the deflection by 8 or 16. Doubling the depth of a rectangular beam divides it by 8. A typical serviceability limit is span/300 for floors and footbridges.

Worked exampleA balcony and a footbridge

E=210 GPa, I=1.8456×107 mm⁴, so EI=3.876×1012 N mm².

  1. Cantilever balcony beam, 1.8 m, 5 kN at the tip: δ=5000⋅18003/(3⋅3.876×1012)=2.51 mm.
  2. Footbridge, simply supported over 6 m, 5 kN/m: δ=5⋅5⋅60004/(384⋅3.876×1012)=21.77 mm, span/276. Slightly over the span/300 target: a deeper section is needed.
  3. The code gets both by integrating M/EI twice, and the footbridge again by solving EIw′′′′=q with finite differences (21.770 mm).
  4. 20 kN at mid-span: PL3/48EI=23.22 mm.

Exercise 1A diving board

A diving board is a cantilever 3 m long, 500 mm wide and 50 mm thick, made of a glass-fibre composite with E=25 GPa. A 750 N diver stands at the tip. How far does it bend?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. I=500⋅503/12=5.208×106 mm⁴, EI=1.302×1011 N mm².
  2. δ=750⋅30003/(3⋅1.302×1011)=51.8 mm.
  3. Bouncing adds dynamic effects (Phase 07), but the static deflection sets the board’s spring stiffness: k=3EI/L3=14.5 N/mm.

06.12.title: Superposition and indeterminate beams
06.12.html:
Most real beams have more supports than statics needs: a floor joist built into a wall at one end, a bridge girder running continuously over several piers. These are indeterminate (05.08), and lesson 06.05 showed the recipe: add compatibility. For beams, the standard deflection formulas plus superposition make it quick.

Superposition

For linear elastic beams with small deflections, the response to several loads is the sum of the responses to each one. That lets you build complicated cases from a table of standard ones.

The method: release, then restore

  1. Release enough supports to make the beam determinate.
  2. Compute the deflection at each released support under the real loads.
  3. Apply the unknown support reaction as a load on the released beam and compute its deflection.
  4. Compatibility: the total deflection at the support must be zero. Solve for the reaction.

Propped cantilever

Clamp at one end, prop at the other, uniform load q. Release the prop. The cantilever tip drops qL4/(8EI); the prop force R lifts it by RL3/(3EI). Setting the sum to zero:

R=83​qL.

The wall takes the other 5qL/8. The bending moment changes completely: from −qL2/2 at the wall of a plain cantilever to −qL2/8, with a sagging peak of 9qL2/128 at 3L/8 from the prop. That’s moment redistribution, and it’s why continuous beams are more efficient than chains of simple spans.

Two equal spans

Remove the middle support of a continuous beam over two spans L: the 2L simple span sags 5q(2L)4/(384EI) at the centre. A central point load R lifts it R(2L)3/(48EI). So the middle support carries R=5qL/4, more than the qL it would carry if the spans were simply supported, and each end carries 3qL/8.

Worked exampleA propped cantilever floor beam

L=4 m, q=5 kN/m, the I-section from 06.10.

  1. Released cantilever tip: qL4/(8EI)=41.28 mm down.
  2. Prop: R=41.28/(L3/3EI)=7.5 kN =3qL/8. Wall: 12.5 kN.
  3. With R applied, the computed tip deflection is −1.6×10−7 mm, zero to numerical accuracy.
  4. Wall moment −10 kN m =−qL2/8; largest sagging moment 5.625 kN m =9qL2/128 at 2.5 m from the wall.
  5. Two spans of 4 m: middle reaction 25 kN =5qL/4, ends 7.5 kN.

Exercise 1A prop under a point load

A cantilever of length L carries a point load P at its free end, which also rests on a prop. What does the prop carry? What if the load is at mid-span instead? (A tip load F at L gives tip deflection FL3/3EI; a load P at L/2 gives a tip deflection of 5PL3/48EI.)

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Load at the tip, right on the prop: the prop carries all of it, R=P. The beam isn’t bent at all.
  2. Load at mid-span: compatibility RL3/(3EI)=5PL3/(48EI), so R=5P/16=0.3125P. The wall takes 11P/16.

06.13.title: Shear stress in beams
06.13.html:
Bending stress gets most of the attention, but beams also carry shear. Short, heavily loaded beams, timber joists near their supports, thin webs of steel girders and glued joints in laminated beams can all fail in shear first. The shear stress is not uniform over the section, and finding where it peaks takes one elegant formula.

Where shear stress comes from

Cut a short slice dx out of a beam where the moment changes from M to M+dM. The bending stresses on the two faces differ slightly. Now cut that slice again horizontally at height y and look at the part above the cut. The unbalanced bending force on it must be carried by a horizontal shear stress on the cut. Working it through (with dM/dx=V) gives Jourawski’s formula:

τ(y)=Ib(y)VQ(y)​,Q(y)=∫ytop​y′dA,

where Q is the first moment, about the neutral axis, of the area above the cut, and b(y) the width at the cut. By the symmetry of shear stresses (06.01), the same τ acts vertically on the cross-section.

Rectangles and I-sections

  • Rectangle: τ is parabolic, zero at the top and bottom, maximum at the neutral axis: τmax​=23​AV​, 50 % above the average.
  • I-section: Q changes little across the web while b is small, so the web carries nearly all the shear at almost uniform stress, about V/(hw​tw​). At the junction with the flange b jumps and τ drops by the ratio of widths.

That’s the division of labour in an I-beam: flanges carry the bending moment (06.10), the web carries the shear.

Worked exampleA joist and an I-beam under 20 kN of shear

  1. Rectangle 50 × 200 mm: τmax​=1.5⋅20000/10000=3.0 MPa at mid-depth. The code integrates τb over the height and gets back exactly 20 kN.
  2. I-section (h=200, flanges 100×8.5, web 5.6 mm): τmax​=20.29 MPa in the web, 15.75 MPa at the web–flange junction, dropping to 0.88 MPa just inside the flange (15.75⋅5.6/100).
  3. The simple estimate V/(hw​tw​)=20000/(183⋅5.6)=19.52 MPa is within 4 %, and the web carries 96.2 % of the shear force.

Exercise 1A glued laminated beam

A glulam beam is 120 mm wide and 400 mm deep, made of 40 mm laminations glued together. The shear force near a support is 60 kN. What shear stress does the glue line at mid-depth carry, and the one 40 mm below the top?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At mid-depth: τ=1.5⋅60000/(120⋅400)=1.875 MPa.
  2. 40 mm below the top: the area above is 120×40 with its centroid 180 mm above the neutral axis, so Q=4800⋅180=8.64×105 mm³. I=120⋅4003/12=6.4×108 mm⁴.
  3. τ=60000⋅8.64×105/(6.4×108⋅120)=0.675 MPa: only 36 % of the mid-depth value.

06.14.title: Torsion of circular shafts
06.14.html:
Every engine, motor and pedal drives something through a twisted shaft: the propeller shaft under a car, the axle of a wind turbine, a screwdriver, a bike’s bottom bracket. Circular shafts are the one torsion problem with a clean exact answer, and it explains why drive shafts are hollow.

Geometry of the twist

Twist a circular shaft by an angle φ over length L. By symmetry, plane cross-sections stay plane and radii stay straight; each section just rotates. A line drawn along the surface becomes a helix. At radius r, the shear strain is

γ=rdxdφ​,

growing linearly from zero at the centre. With Hooke’s law in shear τ=Gγ (06.03), the stress grows linearly too.

Torque and stress

The torque is the sum of τr over the section: T=∫τrdA=Gφ′∫r2dA=GJφ′, with the polar second moment of area J=∫r2dA. So:

τ=JTr​,φ=GJTL​,Jsolid​=32πD4​,Jtube​=32π(D4−d4)​.

GJ is the torsional stiffness, the twin of EI in bending. Stepped shafts add their twists segment by segment.

Why drive shafts are hollow

The material near the centre is barely stressed and adds little to J. Removing it saves weight with only a small loss of strength. Power and torque are linked by P=Tω (Phase 02), so a fast-spinning shaft carries a modest torque for a large power.

Worked exampleA car’s propeller shaft

A hollow steel shaft, 50 mm outside and 42 mm inside, 1.4 m long, carries 1.2 kN m. G=80 GPa.

  1. J=π(504−424)/32=3.081×105 mm⁴ (the code checks it by integrating 2πr3dr).
  2. τmax​=1.2×106⋅25/J=97.37 MPa.
  3. Twist: φ=TL/(GJ)=0.0682 rad =3.905°.
  4. A solid shaft with the same peak stress needs D=(16T/πτ)1/3=39.74 mm, and is 2.15 times heavier.
  5. Stress in that solid shaft at r=0,R/4,R/2,3R/4,R: 0, 24.3, 48.7, 73.0, 97.4 MPa.

Exercise 1A wind turbine low-speed shaft

A small turbine produces 30 kW at 30 rpm. Its hollow shaft has 120 mm outside diameter. If the allowable shear stress is 60 MPa, what is the largest bore?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ω=30⋅2π/60=3.1416 rad/s, so T=30000/3.1416=9549 N m =9.549×106 N mm.
  2. Need J≥T⋅60/60=9.549×106 mm⁴ (with r=60 mm and τ=60 MPa).
  3. π(1204−d4)/32≥9.549×106 gives d4≤2.0736×108−9.727×107=1.1009×108, so d≤102.4 mm.

06.15.title: Thin-walled sections in torsion
06.15.html:
Bike frames, aircraft wings, car chassis rails and box girders all carry torsion in thin walls. For these, whether the section is closed or open matters more than anything else. Take a cardboard tube and twist it: stiff. Slit it along its length and twist again: it gives way like paper. This lesson puts numbers on that.

Closed sections: Bredt’s formula

In a thin closed wall the shear stress is nearly uniform through the thickness. The shear flow q=τt (force per unit length along the wall) turns out to be constant all the way round, even if t varies, by equilibrium of a little piece of wall. Its moment about any point must equal the torque. Since the moment of a constant shear flow round a closed loop is q⋅2Am​, where Am​ is the area enclosed by the mid-line:

q=2Am​T​,τ=2Am​tT​,J=∮ds/t4Am2​​.

These are the Bredt–Batho formulas. For a circular tube they agree with the exact J within a fraction of a percent.

Open sections

An open thin section (a slit tube, a channel, an I-beam) can’t sustain a circulating shear flow. Each wall twists on its own, with the stress reversing through the thickness, like a thin flat strip:

J≈∑3bt3​,τmax​=JTt​.

Thickness enters cubed and the enclosed area doesn’t appear at all. For a circular tube of mean radius rm​, the ratio closed/open is 3(rm​/t)2: hundreds of times stiffer for typical tubes.

Design consequences

  • Members that carry torsion should be closed: tubes, boxes, torsion boxes in wings.
  • Open sections (I-beams, channels) are excellent in bending and poor in torsion. Loads that twist them should be avoided or they need bracing.
  • A car’s floor pan becomes stiff in torsion when the sills, tunnels and roof form closed loops.

Worked exampleA bike down tube, closed and slit

Aluminium (G=26 GPa) tube, 35 mm outside, 1.2 mm wall: rm​=16.9 mm, Am​=897.3 mm².

  1. Bredt: J=4Am2​/(2πrm​/t)=3.639×104 mm⁴, against an exact thick-wall J of 3.644×104 (0.13 % low).
  2. Slit: J=2πrm​t3/3=61.16 mm⁴. Closed/open = 595, which equals 3(rm​/t)2.
  3. Under 60 N m: closed τ=T/(2Am​t)=27.86 MPa; slit τ=Tt/J=1177 MPa, 42 times higher. The slit tube would fail long before the closed one notices the load.
  4. A box 120 × 60 × 3 mm: J=1.534×106 mm⁴ and τ=25.0 MPa at 1 kN m.

Exercise 1A square tube against a channel

A square steel tube is 50 × 50 mm with 2 mm walls, under 200 N m. Find its shear stress and J. Then imagine cutting one wall along its length to make an open section with the same walls. What are J and the stress now?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Mid-line square 48 × 48 mm: Am​=2304 mm², ∮ds/t=4⋅48/2=96.
  2. Closed: J=4⋅23042/96=2.212×105 mm⁴; τ=200000/(2⋅2304⋅2)=21.7 MPa.
  3. Open: J=4⋅48⋅23/3=512 mm⁴, 432 times less; τ=200000⋅2/512=781 MPa, beyond the yield strength of most steels.
